stops.before: A hundred and twenty people in an upper room, praying, with Mary among them. It is the feast of the giving of the Law on Sinai.
stops.watch: Tongues of fire; Peter, who hid from a servant girl seven weeks ago, preaching to thousands — and three thousand baptised; the believers holding all things in common; the lame man at the Beautiful Gate: 'Silver and gold I have none.' The Sanhedrin cannot stop them: 'we cannot but speak.'
stops.after: The first martyr, and the persecution that spreads the Gospel by scattering it.

stops.before: Ananias and Sapphira have died for a lie; seven deacons are chosen to serve tables, and one of them cannot stop preaching.
stops.watch: Stephen's speech, the whole Old Testament retold as a story of a stiff-necked people, ending 'I see the heavens opened'; the stones; the young man minding the coats, named Saul. Then Philip in Samaria, and the Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot.
stops.after: Saul, breathing threats, takes the road to Damascus.

stops.before: The Church's most dangerous enemy is thrown to the ground by a light and a voice.
stops.watch: Three days blind; Ananias's fear; the basket down the wall. Peter's vision of the sheet of unclean animals and Cornelius the centurion — the door opened to the Gentiles. Antioch, where they are first called Christians; James killed; Peter freed by an angel while the church prays, and the girl who leaves him standing at the gate.
stops.after: The church at Antioch lays hands on Barnabas and Saul and sends them west.

stops.before: Cyprus, Galatia, then — after a vision of a man of Macedonia — Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Athens, Corinth.
stops.watch: The Council of Jerusalem in chapter 15, which decides that Gentiles need not become Jews — the hinge of the book. Paul and Silas singing in the Philippian jail; the Areopagus speech to the philosophers ('to the unknown God'); Corinth, where he stays eighteen months. Galatians and the Thessalonian letters are written on these roads: 'it is no longer I that live, but Christ liveth in me.'
stops.after: Three years in Ephesus, and letters to a church that is tearing itself apart.

stops.before: From Ephesus, where the silversmiths riot for Diana, Paul writes to the Corinthians about factions, lawsuits, immorality, the Eucharist, and a resurrection some of them doubt.
stops.watch: 'The word of the cross is foolishness to them that perish'; the Lord's Supper as he received it; the body and its members; the hymn to charity (13); and chapter 15, 'if Christ be not risen, your faith is vain'. Then Romans, his summa, written from Corinth: all have sinned; justified by faith; nothing can separate us from the love of God (8).
stops.after: He goes up to Jerusalem knowing what waits there.

stops.before: Arrested in the Temple on a false charge, rescued by Roman soldiers from a lynch mob, Paul appeals to Caesar.
stops.watch: His defence on the fortress steps; the plot of forty men; two years in Caesarea; the shipwreck on Malta, told by Luke who was aboard; and Rome, under house arrest, 'preaching the kingdom with all confidence, without prohibition'. From that house: Philippians' hymn — 'he emptied himself' — and Ephesians on the Church as his body and bride.
stops.after: Last letters, from Paul and from Peter, as Nero's fire lights the city.

stops.t: I have fought the good fight
stops.before: Paul writes to Timothy from his last prison; Peter writes to the churches of Asia as 'a witness of the sufferings of Christ'. Both die under Nero.
stops.watch: 'I have finished my course, I have kept the faith'; Peter's 'a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood'; James's faith without works is dead, and the tongue as a fire; Hebrews' roll-call of faith (11) and 'a cloud of witnesses'. The pastoral letters build the church that will outlive the apostles: bishops, deacons, widows, sound doctrine.
stops.after: Jerusalem falls to Titus in 70, as Jesus said. One apostle remains, very old, on an island.
